scenario: AITA for my gf and I keeping our income low to apply for lower income housing. | Ok so this is weird. My girlfriend and I have been looking to move in together so we’ve been searching for apartments. My parents recently onformed me that they’d be moving to Phoenix, AZ in August so I would need to find my own place. A lot of the apartments were too expensive for our budget but we found 1 that we’re happy with. The complex was very nice and the lost cost we were told was 890/mo for 1 bed/1 bath. We were also informed of this application where if you and whoever are living in the apartment are making less than 32000 collectively a year then you apply for the “bond program” (I think it was called) that let’s you live in their studio apartments for less rent (about 550 a month not including utilities) We asked about the availability of the apartment and they told us that there are a lot available right now so it’s not like people are scrambling to get in. My gf has been looking for a new job and would like to switch to full time when she finishes college. I told her that she should wait until we apply and get the verification that we apply for the program to actually go full time and she agreed. We wouldn’t apply until July. (She’s not struggling for cash or anything and i would help out if that ever were the case, this would strictly be to save money in the long run). We also started trying to attack our debts together and would be basically living like poor people for the foreseeable future until we were out of debt. So this program would give us a head start. After the leasing period, if your income rises above 32000 a year you’d be asked to move into the normal studio (which is the same size and specs as the bond program one). We cooould afford to live in the normal apartments comfortably but it would take longer to pay off our debts. AITA?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Honesty and integrity matter in relationships (including with landlords/communities). - *For*: If you’re transparent with your landlord (e.g., "We’re applying for the program now but plan to transition later"), it might feel less exploitative. 4. **Social Contract** - Housing programs exist to **level the playing field** for those who can’t compete in the market. But if others are denied access because of your application, that’s a problem. - **Alternatives**: Could you afford the regular unit *now* without sacrificing debt repayment? If yes, why not just pay the extra $340/month to avoid this dilemma? --- ### **My Personal Take (0.5/1)** I’d rate this **0.5/1**—**not wrong, but questionable**. Here’s why: - **Not "wrong" in a legal sense**: If the program has no income checks until after the lease, you’re not breaking rules. But **ethically, it’s shady**. - **Intent matters**: If you’re doing this to **genuinely help yourselves** (not to "game the system"), it’s less condemnable. But if others could use the spot more, it’s unfair. - **Better alternatives exist**: If you can afford the regular unit *without* cutting back on debt repayment, why not? The extra $340/month is a small price for peace of mind. - **Relationship impact**: If your girlfriend is on board, that’s good. But if she’s pressured or uncomfortable, that’s a red flag. --- ### **What I’d Do** 1. **Be transparent**: Tell the landlord, *"We’re applying for the program now but expect to move to a regular unit later when our income increases."* This makes it less exploitative. 2. **Ask about waitlists**: If the program has a long waitlist, maybe others *need* the spot more than you do. 3. **Reevaluate debt vs. housing**: Could you afford the regular unit *and* still attack debt aggressively? If yes, skip the program. 4. **Consider the bigger picture**: If you’re in a position to afford housing now, is this really a "hardship"? If not, the answer might be **no**. --- ### **Final Verdict** This isn’t *morally wrong* in a criminal sense, but it’s **ethically questionable**—especially if others could benefit more. If you’re doing it **only to save money** (not because you’re truly struggling), it feels like **taking advantage of a system meant for others**. Would I call it "wrong"? **Not legally.** Would I call it **dishonest or unfair**? **Yes.** Would I do it? **Only if I were in a genuine bind and had no other options.** Would you like help brainstorming alternatives that keep you on the ethical high road?
